Foundation
Foundation: understanding the ICPs
Start with the purpose of insurance supervision, how the ICPs fit together, and the difference between principles, standards and guidance.
Think of the principles as the destination, the standards as the essential requirements, and the guidance as help with getting there.
Objectives & powers
Objectives, powers and responsibilities of the supervisor
Effective supervision starts with a clear mandate. The authorities responsible for insurance supervision need clearly defined objectives, responsibilities and legal powers.
Before a supervisor can require an insurer to take action, its authority and responsibilities need to be established in law.
The supervisor
Supervisor
A supervisor needs operational independence, accountability, transparency and sufficient resources to carry out its responsibilities effectively.
A supervisory decision should be based on the supervisor’s mandate, rather than pressure from an insurer or another interested party.
Information sharing
Information sharing and confidentiality requirements
Supervisors need to obtain and exchange relevant information while protecting confidential material and respecting restrictions on its purpose and use.
Two supervisors may need to exchange non-public information about an insurance group, using safeguards for how that information is handled.
Licensing
Licensing
Licensing is a first checkpoint for entering the insurance market. Supervisors assess whether applicants can meet the requirements to operate and fulfil obligations to policyholders.
A company’s business registration alone does not establish that it is authorised to carry on insurance activities.
Suitability of people
Suitability of persons
People who direct, oversee or control an insurer need to be suitable for their roles. Competence, integrity and, for significant owners, financial soundness matter.
When assessing a proposed director, relevant experience matters alongside integrity and the ability to carry out the role.
Control & transfers
Change of control and portfolio transfers
Changes in who controls an insurer, and transfers of insurance portfolios, require supervisory assessment. Oversight should remain effective as ownership or business arrangements change.
An acquisition that gives a new owner control of an insurer is a supervisory concern, even when the insurer’s name stays the same.
Corporate governance
Corporate governance
Governance sets out how an insurer is directed and overseen. Clear responsibilities, prudent decision-making and effective oversight help protect policyholders.
A board needs to oversee major business decisions and hold management accountable, rather than simply approve every proposal.
Risk & internal controls
Risk management and internal controls
Insurers need effective systems to identify and manage risk, supported by internal controls and appropriate control functions. These systems should evolve with the business.
A growing insurer may need stronger controls and additional risk expertise as it introduces new products or enters new markets.
Review & reporting
Supervisory review and reporting
Supervision is an ongoing process. Reporting, off-site monitoring and on-site inspections help supervisors understand insurers, assess risks and follow up on concerns.
An unusual movement in reported claims may prompt questions, closer analysis or an on-site inspection.
Measures & sanctions
Preventive measures, corrective measures and sanctions
Supervisors need to act promptly when problems emerge. Preventive action seeks to avoid breaches, corrective action responds to problems, and sanctions address violations.
A supervisor may require an insurer to fix weaknesses before they put policyholders at greater risk.
Exit & resolution
Exit from the market and resolution
An insurer’s exit needs a clear framework. Resolution arrangements should help deal with insurers in difficulty while protecting policyholders and considering financial stability.
When an insurer can no longer remain viable, authorities need tools and arrangements to manage the situation in an orderly way.
Reinsurance & risk transfer
Reinsurance and other forms of risk transfer
Reinsurance and other risk-transfer arrangements can help an insurer manage exposures. Supervisors assess whether these arrangements are effective and appropriately managed.
Passing part of a large exposure to a reinsurer can reduce risk, but it also creates exposure to that reinsurer.
Valuation
Valuation
Consistent valuation of assets and liabilities supports a meaningful view of an insurer’s financial position and solvency. Assumptions and methods need to reflect the relevant risks.
Changing an assumption about future claims can affect the value of insurance liabilities and the assessment of solvency.
Investments
Investments
Investment requirements help ensure that insurers manage investment risks appropriately for solvency purposes, taking account of the obligations those assets support.
An insurer should consider whether its investments can support claim payments when they fall due, rather than focus only on return.
Enterprise risk management
Enterprise risk management for solvency purposes
Enterprise risk management connects risk, strategy and capital. It helps an insurer understand its overall risk profile and its ability to meet obligations over time.
Before expanding into a new line of business, an insurer considers how the added risks affect its strategy and capital needs.
Capital adequacy
Capital adequacy
Capital requirements help insurers absorb significant unexpected losses. Solvency assessment considers assets, liabilities, risks and available capital together.
A severe loss can test whether an insurer has sufficient financial resources beyond the amounts set aside for expected obligations.
Intermediaries
Intermediaries
Supervision of intermediaries supports professional and transparent insurance distribution. Requirements apply to relevant organisations and individuals involved in intermediation.
A broker placing insurance for a customer should conduct that business professionally and transparently.
Conduct of business
Conduct of business
Fair treatment of customers matters throughout the insurance relationship, from product design and sales through to claims, complaints and the fulfilment of obligations.
Clear information at the point of sale is only one part of fair treatment; claims and complaints also need fair and timely handling.
Public disclosure
Public disclosure
Timely, relevant disclosures help policyholders and market participants understand an insurer’s activities, risks, performance and financial position.
A useful disclosure gives readers a clear view of significant risks, rather than presenting financial results without context.
Countering fraud
Countering fraud in insurance
Insurers and intermediaries need effective measures to deter, prevent, detect, report and remedy insurance fraud. Fraud can harm both firms and policyholders.
A pattern of suspicious claims may require investigation, but fraud controls also need to address risks involving staff and intermediaries.
Anti-money laundering
Anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism
Insurers, intermediaries and supervisors need effective measures to address money laundering and terrorist financing risks in the insurance sector.
An unusual transaction may call for closer scrutiny under the applicable anti-money laundering controls.
Group-wide supervision
Group-wide supervision
A supervisor needs a view of the insurance group as a whole. Defining the group and the scope of supervision helps avoid gaps or unnecessary duplication.
A risk arising elsewhere in a corporate group may affect its insurance business, even if that business appears sound on its own.
Macroprudential supervision
Macroprudential supervision
Macroprudential supervision looks beyond individual firms to sector-wide vulnerabilities, shared exposures and risks that can affect the wider financial system.
Many insurers holding similar assets may be exposed to the same market shock, making a sector-wide view valuable.
Cooperation & coordination
Supervisory cooperation and coordination
Supervisors need to cooperate and coordinate, particularly where groups operate across borders. Agreed arrangements help support effective group-wide supervision.
Supervisors in different countries may use a supervisory college to discuss a cross-border insurance group and coordinate their work.
